title: Yusuf Ansari
text:
Hi there, I’m Yusuf Ansari.
I am a biostatistician in the Department of Data Science at the University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) and a PhD student (PT) with research interests in longitudinal data analysis, survival analysis, joint models, and statistical computing.
My collaborative research has included work with the Department of Pediatrics at UMMC, the MIND Center at UMMC, and the Jackson Heart Study (JHS), spanning a variety of biomedical and clinical research questions.

title: GLM Diagnostics in R
text: In this post, we are going to discuss the diagnostic measures of Generalized Linear Model (GLM). We will start by stating the assumptions of GLM. Then, we are going to simulate fake data from binary logistic regression model. Then, we construct a wrong model by misspecifying certain parts of the model. We will use these models to show how various residual procedure are used to identify any model misfit. But, before that, different types of residuals will be discussed followed by leverages in GLM. Graphical plots will be used to check the model assumptions. A brief introduction of outliers and influential measures will be carried out before discussing the remedial measures.

title: GLM Diagnostics in R
text:
4.1 Response Residuals (Rr)
Response Residual is the difference between the response yi and \(\mu_i\), i.e. Rri = yi - \(\hat\mu_i\).

fit = predict(m1, type = "response")
head(y-fit)

           1            2            3            4            5            6 
2.722883e-06 2.131567e-03 5.630650e-01 4.550829e-01 1.419348e-01 2.209112e-02 


Alternative approach using the residuals() function.
residuals(m1, type = "response") %>% head()
For linear model, Rr need to be normally distributed with mean 0 and constant variance. For GLM, it’s not necessarily true always.

rr = residuals(m1, type = "response")
qqnorm(rr)
qqline(rr)




We need the Rr to behave like the Rr in linear model, so that we can evaluate our GLM model fit. But, the above qqnorm plot of the correct model tells us that the Rr in GLM are not following normal distribution. This type of residuals are not sufficient for assessing GLM model fit and hence a modification is required.

title: GLM Diagnostics in R
text:
4.2 Pearson Residuals (Pr)
Pearson residuals (Pr) are defined as the difference between the observed and expected responses and divided by the square root of the estimated variance of \(y_i\). Mathematically, \[ \Pr_i = \frac{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)} {\sqrt{\hat Var(\\y_i)}} \] For logistic regression, \(\Pr_i = \frac{y_i - \hat p_i} {\sqrt{\hat p_i (1-\hat p_i)}}\).
For poisson regression, \(\Pr_i = \frac{y_i - e^{x_i\hat \beta_i}} {\sqrt{e^{x_i\hat \beta_i}}}\).


Note: \(\sum \Pr_i^2 = \frac{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2} {\hat Var(\\y_i)}.\) When the GLM is the model corresponding to independence for cells in a two-way contingency table, this is the Pearson Chi-squared statistic \(\chi^2\) for testing independence. (“Generalized Linear Models,” n.d.)
The following plot is showing that Pearson residuals deviate from normality when it comes from logistic regression model.

pr = residuals(m1, type = "pearson")
qqnorm(pr)
qqline(pr)



# plot(m1)


4.2.1 Standardized Pearson Residual (spr):
The denominator of the pearson residual accounts for the variability in \(y_i\), but not for the variability for \(\hat \mu_i\). The spr solves this issue by dividing \((y_i - \hat \mu_i)\) by its standard error, SE. Mathematically, \[
spr = \frac{(y_i - \hat \mu_i)} {SE} = \frac{(y_i - \hat \mu_i)} {\sqrt{\hat Var(y_i)(1-h_i)}};   
\] here \(h_i\) represents leverage.



pr1 = residuals(m1, type = "pearson")/sqrt(1 - hatvalues(m1))
qqnorm(pr1)
qqline(pr1)
